content: Salivary gland enlargement can occur due to a variety of causes, ranging from life-threatening conditions to more common or localized issues. Life-Threatening Causes of Salivary Gland Enlargement: 1. Carcinoma: Malignant tumors originating in the salivary glands can lead to significant gland enlargement and may metastasize to other areas. 2. Cirrhosis of the Liver: Advanced liver disease can cause systemic effects, including salivary gland swelling. 3. Lymphoma: This hematologic malignancy can involve the salivary glands, leading to their enlargement. 4. Malignant Salivary Gland Tumors: Aggressive cancers of the salivary glands, such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma or adenoid cystic carcinoma, can cause progressive glandular swelling. 5. Parotid Adenoma and Parotid Cancer: Tumors of the parotid gland, whether benign or malignant, can result in noticeable enlargement. 6. Renal Failure: Chronic kidney disease can lead to metabolic disturbances that may manifest as salivary gland swelling. 7. Septicemia and Severe Infections: Systemic infections can cause inflammation and swelling of the salivary glands as part of a generalized inflammatory response. Common Causes of Salivary Gland Enlargement: 1. Acromegaly: Excess growth hormone can lead to hypertrophy of various tissues, including the salivary glands. 2. Amyloidosis: Deposition of amyloid proteins in the salivary glands can cause their enlargement. 3. Anorexia Nervosa: Chronic malnutrition and purging behaviors can lead to parotid gland swelling. 4. Bacterial Infections: Acute or chronic bacterial sialadenitis can cause painful glandular swelling. 5. Chronic Sialadenitis: Recurrent or persistent inflammation of the salivary glands can lead to their enlargement. 6. Cirrhosis: Liver dysfunction can result in secondary effects on the salivary glands. 7. Cytomegalovirus (CMV): Viral infections, including CMV, can involve the salivary glands. 8. Coxsackie Virus: This viral infection can cause inflammation and swelling of the salivary glands. 9. Drug-Induced Enlargement: Certain medications, such as pergolide, can cause salivary gland swelling as a side effect. 10. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): This virus, associated with infectious mononucleosis, can lead to salivary gland involvement. 11. HIV: Salivary gland enlargement is a recognized feature in some individuals with HIV. 12. Hyperlipidemia: Elevated lipid levels can sometimes be associated with salivary gland swelling. 13. Mumps: This viral infection primarily affects the parotid glands, causing painful swelling. 14. Sarcoidosis: This granulomatous disease can involve the salivary glands, leading to their enlargement. 15. Tuberculosis: Mycobacterial infections can occasionally involve the salivary glands. Causes by Organ System: 1. Alcoholism: Chronic alcohol use can lead to parotid gland enlargement. 2. Allergic Sialadenitis: Allergic reactions can cause inflammation and swelling of the salivary glands. 3. Benign Adenomas: Non-cancerous tumors of the salivary glands can cause localized swelling. 4. Bulimia Nervosa: Repeated vomiting can lead to parotid gland hypertrophy. 5. Cystic Fibrosis: This genetic condition can affect the salivary glands, leading to enlargement. 6. Growth Hormone-Secreting Pituitary Adenoma: Excess growth hormone can cause salivary gland hypertrophy. 7. Heerfordt-Waldenström Syndrome: A rare manifestation of sarcoidosis involving the parotid glands, uveitis, and fever. 8. Lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes near the salivary glands can mimic glandular swelling. 9. Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonia: This condition can involve the salivary glands, particularly in the context of autoimmune diseases. 10. Malabsorption Syndromes: Nutritional deficiencies can lead to secondary effects on the salivary glands. 11. Mikulicz Syndrome: A condition characterized by bilateral, painless enlargement of the salivary and lacrimal glands, often associated with autoimmune diseases. 12. Necrotizing Sialometaplasia: A benign, self-limiting condition presenting as a painful ulcer of the hard palate, often mistaken for malignancy. 13. Pancreatitis: Inflammatory conditions of the pancreas can have systemic effects, including salivary gland involvement. 14. Poor Dental Hygiene: Chronic oral infections can lead to secondary salivary gland inflammation. 15. Post-Surgical Infections: Infections following head and neck surgeries can involve the salivary glands. 16. Propylthiouracil: This medication, used to treat hyperthyroidism, can cause salivary gland swelling as a side effect. 17. Salivary Stones (Sialolithiasis): Obstruction of salivary ducts by stones can lead to glandular swelling and pain. 18. Sjögren’s Syndrome: An autoimmune disorder characterized by dry eyes, dry mouth, and salivary gland enlargement. 19. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus Infections: Bacterial infections can cause acute or chronic sialadenitis. 20. Viral Infections: Various viral pathogens can involve the salivary glands, leading to swelling. Normal Salivary Glands: The salivary glands include the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands. The submandibular ducts (Wharton’s ducts) open into the floor of the mouth at the lingual caruncles, located near the base of the tongue. Pathological Findings: 1. Mixed Tumors of the Parotid: These tumors often present as painless, slow-growing masses. Recurrent mixed tumors may exhibit multinodular growth. 2. Canalicular Adenoma: Over 70% of these benign tumors occur in the upper lip. 3. Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma: These tumors often appear as bluish, fluctuant lesions on the palate, mimicking mucous retention cysts. 4. Acinic Cell Adenocarcinoma: Typically presents as a subcutaneous nodule near the ear, often involving the superficial lobe of the parotid gland. 5. Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma: A slow-growing tumor that can present as a lobulated mass in the anterior floor of the mouth. 6. Polymorphous Low-Grade Adenocarcinoma: Presents as a well-circumscribed mass at the junction of the hard and soft palates, often with telangiectasia of the overlying mucosa. 7. Necrotizing Sialometaplasia: Commonly presents as a slow-healing ulcer of the hard palate, often preceded by swelling. 8. Mucocele: A smooth, dome-shaped nodule, often found on the lower lip, caused by mucous extravasation. 9. Ranula: A type of mucocele occurring in the floor of the mouth, either as an extravasation or retention cyst. 10. Ruptured Mucocele: Trauma, such as lip biting, can cause rupture and collapse of mucoceles. 11. Superficial Mucocele: Appears translucent due to the thin overlying mucosa. This detailed description provides a comprehensive understanding of the various causes and presentations of salivary gland enlargement, as well as the associated pathological findings.
